summary.text: At \(n=67\), the distinct values \(m=147\) and \(m=2055\) both contribute: their residue lists modulo successive powers of two are respectively \((1,3,3,3,19,19,19)\) and \((1,3,7,7,7,7,7,7,7,7,7)\), each summing to \(67\). Since both lie below the sufficient bound \(2^{68}\), the number of occurrences at \(67\) is at least two, contradicting the claimed value one.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor \log_2 m\rfloor}(m\bmod 2^k),
\]
where \(m\bmod 2^k\) is the least nonnegative residue of \(m\) modulo \(2^k\). Thus \(F\) is sequence A049802, and \(a(n)\), sequence A383327, is the number of integers \(m\) for which \(F(m)=n\).

We disprove the conjecture at the listed value \(n=67\). It suffices to exhibit two distinct integers \(m\) for which \(F(m)=67\). We will use
\[
m_1=147\qquad\text{and}\qquad m_2=2055.
\]

First consider \(m_1=147\). Since
\[
2^7=128\le 147<256=2^8,
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 147\rfloor=7\). Its residues modulo the powers \(2^k\), for \(1\le k\le 7\), are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
k&2^k&147\bmod 2^k\\ \hline
1&2&1\\
2&4&3\\
3&8&3\\
4&16&3\\
5&32&19\\
6&64&19\\
7&128&19
\end{array}
\]
Indeed, the first four entries follow from \(147=144+3\), with \(144\) divisible by \(2,4,8,16\) except that modulo \(2\) the residue of the odd number \(147\) is \(1\); and the last three follow from \(147=128+19\), with \(128\) divisible by \(32,64,128\). Consequently,
\[
F(147)=1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67.
\]

Now consider \(m_2=2055\). Since
\[
2^{11}=2048\le 2055<4096=2^{12},
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 2055\rfloor=11\). Also
\[
2055=2048+7=2^{11}+7.
\]
Therefore its residues are
\[
2055\bmod 2=1,
\qquad
2055\bmod 4=3,
\]
and
\[
2055\bmod 2^k=7\quad\text{for every }k=3,4,\ldots,11.
\]
For \(k=3,\ldots,11\), this last assertion holds because \(2^k\) divides \(2^{11}=2048\), while \(0\le 7<2^k\). There are nine values of \(k\) from \(3\) through \(11\). Hence
\[
F(2055)=1+3+9\cdot 7=4+63=67.
\]

Thus both \(147\) and \(2055\) are indices at which A049802 has value \(67\). They are distinct, so the number of occurrences of \(67\) is at least two:
\[
a(67)\ge 2.
\]

Equivalently, if one uses the finite counting range \(0\le m<2^{67+1}=2^{68}\) supplied by the standard bound for this sequence, both witnesses are included: indeed,
\[
147<2055<2^{12}<2^{68}.
\]
Thus even within that finite range the set of indices producing \(67\) contains the two-element subset \(\{147,2055\}\), and therefore its cardinality is at least two. In particular it cannot have cardinality one.

Finally, \(67\) belongs to the conjecture's specified set
\[
\{1,3,5,9,15,23,35,63,65,67\}.
\]
The conjecture asserts, among other things, that \(a(67)=1\), whereas the two explicit occurrences above give \(a(67)\ge 2\). This contradiction disproves the conjecture.
